subject: language_arts

unit.title: Comprehension & composition
unit.essentialQuestion: How do I read between the lines, and how do I write a clear set of instructions?

title: Inference with a clue (and proving it)
objectives: By the end, I can make an inference and back it up with a clue from the text.

vocabulary.definition: work out something the text doesn't say, using clues
vocabulary.example: The text says Tom's hands shook — I infer he is scared.

vocabulary.definition: the words that leak the hidden answer
vocabulary.example: 'skipped' and 'huge grin' are clues that Mai is happy.

vocabulary.definition: the clue you point to that proves your idea
vocabulary.example: My evidence is 'his hands were shaking'.

vocabulary.definition: show your idea is right by giving the clue
vocabulary.example: I prove it with 'because the text says…'.

emphasize: An inference has TWO parts: what you think AND the clue — always 'I think… because the text says…'.
A feeling with no clue is just a guess. Detectives prove it.
Pre-empt clue-dodging: the clue must come from the TEXT, not from memory or opinion.

keyConcepts: inferring an unstated feeling from clue words
backing every inference with quoted evidence
the answer stem 'I think… because the text says…'
misconceptions: giving a feeling with no clue — a guess dressed as an inference
answering from opinion or personal memory instead of the text ('I'd be excited, so he is')
retelling the whole passage instead of pointing to the ONE clue that shows the feeling
picking a clue that doesn't match the feeling claimed
hooks: The text never says 'scared' — but we KNOW Tom is. How? The clues leak it.
priorKnowledge: clue and evidence as detective words

digital: the 'I think… because the text says…' stem card

video.watchTask: Every time the teacher makes an inference, shout out the CLUE before they say it.

afterCheck.question: What two parts does a good inference answer have?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: What I think AND the clue from the text ('because the text says…').

plan.goal: Present the Tom sentence — the word 'scared' is never written, yet we all KNOW — and retrieve Lesson 21's find-it vs work-it-out.
plan.note: Read the Tom line with feeling, then pause. Let the mystery land before explaining anything.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'How does Tom feel?' is a work-it-out (inference) question.

script.say: Read this with me: 'Tom's hands were shaking and he couldn't speak.' It never uses the word scared — but we just KNOW he is. Spooky, right? How do we know? The clues tell us. Today, detective, we don't just crack the hidden feeling — we PROVE it with evidence. Quick warm-up: is 'How does Tom feel?' a find-it question or a work-it-out question?
script.adaptHints: Read the Tom line in a hushed, dramatic voice. If the child loves a particular story hero, say 'even [hero] would need clues for this one.'

blocks.markdown:
**The mystery sentence**

Tom stood at the classroom door. His hands were shaking and he couldn't speak.

blocks.caption: The word 'scared' is never written… so how do we KNOW?

stuckProtocol: If 'inference' doesn't come back: 'Can you put your finger on the word scared? No? Then it's a work-it-out — an inference.'

plan.goal: Model the two-part proof: I think Tom is SCARED (what I think) BECAUSE THE TEXT SAYS his hands were shaking (the clue). Introduce the stem.
plan.note: Say the full stem sentence slowly, twice. The stem is the lesson's tool — the child should be able to chant it by the end of this beat.
plan.successCriteria: Child can repeat the stem 'I think… because the text says…' and name its two parts.

script.say: Here's how a detective PROVES an inference. Watch my two parts. Part one — what I think: I think Tom is SCARED. Part two — the clue: BECAUSE THE TEXT SAYS his hands were shaking and he couldn't speak. See? What I think, AND the clue. I always use the magic stem: 'I think… because the text says…'. Say the stem with me — twice!
script.adaptHints: Chant the stem rhythmically. If the learner responds to superheroes, call the stem their 'power move'.

blocks.definition: I think… because the text says…
blocks.example: I think Tom is scared because the text says his hands were shaking.

blocks.title: Prove an inference in two parts
steps: Part 1 — what I think: 'I think Tom is scared…'
Part 2 — the clue: '…because the text says his hands were shaking and he couldn't speak.'

plan.goal: Shared inference on the Mai passage: child names the feeling AND finds the clue words; build the stem sentence together.
plan.note: The child supplies both parts; the character scribes. Accept 'happy/excited/joyful' — the clue is what matters.
plan.successCriteria: Child says Mai is happy and points to 'skipped' and 'huge grin' as the clues, then completes the stem.

script.say: New case! 'Mai skipped to school with a huge grin.' How does Mai feel, detective — and what's our clue? Don't just tell me the feeling… point me to the words that leak it. Then let's build the full proof sentence together: I think Mai is… because the text says…
script.adaptHints: If the child gives the feeling without the clue, don't accept it yet: 'Nearly a proof! Which words leaked it?'

blocks.markdown:
**Case two: Mai**

Mai skipped to school with a huge grin. She waved at everyone she passed.

blocks.text: I think Mai is happy ___ the text says she skipped and had a huge grin.

check.question: How do we know Tom is scared?
check.expectedAnswer: Because the text says his hands were shaking and he couldn't speak — those are the clues.

wrongAnswers.answer: Because he just is / I can tell
wrongAnswers.why: inference without evidence — a guess
wrongAnswers.remedy: What in the TEXT made you think it? Point to the words and add 'because the text says…'.

wrongAnswers.answer: Because the text says he is scared
wrongAnswers.why: believes the answer is written — retrieval habit
wrongAnswers.remedy: Hunt for the word 'scared' in the sentence. Not there! So which words LEAK the fear instead?

plan.goal: Solo proof: the child answers 'How does Leo feel?' with the full stem — feeling + matching clue.
plan.note: This is the lesson's key diagnostic. Both parts must appear. A feeling alone, or a retell of the whole passage, doesn't pass.
plan.successCriteria: Child produces a full stem sentence: a sensible feeling + a clue quoted or located from the text.

script.say: Your solo case. 'Leo dragged his feet all the way home. His kite was in bits in his bag.' How does Leo feel? Answer like a detective — the FULL proof: 'I think… because the text says…'.
script.adaptHints: Probe after success: 'Which words exactly are your clue?' Accept sad/upset/disappointed — any feeling the clues support.

blocks.markdown:
**Case three: Leo**

Leo dragged his feet all the way home. His kite was in bits in his bag.

blocks.prompt: How does Leo feel? Prove it: 'I think… because the text says…'
blocks.sample: I think Leo feels sad because the text says he dragged his feet and his kite was in bits.

check.question: How does Leo feel — with your proof?
check.expectedAnswer: I think Leo feels sad/disappointed because the text says he dragged his feet and his kite was in bits.

wrongAnswers.why: feeling with no evidence — guessing
wrongAnswers.remedy: I believe you — now PROVE it. What in the text made you think that? Add 'because the text says…'.

wrongAnswers.answer: He walked home and his kite broke and he was walking slowly and…
wrongAnswers.why: retells the whole passage instead of picking the one clue
wrongAnswers.remedy: Just the one clue that shows the feeling — which words leak the sadness most?

wrongAnswers.answer: I think Leo is happy because the text says he had a kite
wrongAnswers.why: clue doesn't match the feeling — evidence and idea disagree
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check your clue against your idea: dragging feet, kite in BITS — do those words leak happy? What do they leak?

plan.goal: Independent inference proofs across fresh mini-passages: feeling + clue every time, using the stem.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Never accept part one without part two. Interleave a clue-spotting MC between written proofs to keep pace.
plan.successCriteria: Child completes 3+ items with both parts present and clues that match the feelings.

script.say: Detective casebook open! Quick cases, one after another. For every one: what you think, AND the clue. No proof, no badge!
script.adaptHints: Swap the reward flavour (badge, star, case file) to the child's interests. Passages and answers never change.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'your idea is missing its clue' or 'your clue doesn't match your idea'.
Highlight the clue words together in the passage.
One hint: 'Finish the sentence: because the text says…'.
Re-ask with an easy, loud clue (Mai's huge grin), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states the two parts of a good inference answer and says the stem aloud; end on a win.
plan.note: Child-led. Listen for both halves: what I think + the clue.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'what I think AND the clue — because the text says…'.

script.say: Casebook closed! Tell me, detective: what two parts does a good inference answer have? … Exactly. You proved your ideas with clues from the text every time — that's exactly how strong readers think.
script.adaptHints: Praise the observed process: quoting clues, matching clue to feeling. Never 'clever' — always the strategy.

blocks.prompt: Say the proof stem out loud one more time, like you're teaching it to a friend.
blocks.target: I think… because the text says…

practiceBank.skill: infer a feeling from clue words

block.prompt: 'Mai skipped to school with a huge grin.' How does Mai feel?
block.explain: Skipping and a huge grin are what happy looks like — those words leak the feeling.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't read the clue words — answered at random
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at what Mai DOES: skipping, grinning. Act it out — does your face feel sad doing that?

wrongAnswers.why: guessing without checking the clues
wrongAnswers.remedy: Which words show what Mai is doing? Do scared people skip and grin?

hints: Look at what Mai DOES: skipped… huge grin…
Act the clue out — what feeling fits it?

reteach.say: Feelings leak through actions. Read the actions, feel the feeling: SKIPPED — bouncy! HUGE GRIN — beaming! Put them together and the hidden word appears: happy. The text never says it; the clues shout it.

practiceBank.skill: spot the clue that proves a feeling

block.prompt: We think Tom is scared. Which words are the CLUE?
options: 'His hands were shaking and he couldn't speak'
block.explain: Shaking hands and a stuck voice are what fear looks like — that's the evidence.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: 'His hands were shaking and he couldn't speak'

wrongAnswers.why: chose the setting, not the behaviour that shows the feeling
wrongAnswers.remedy: Standing at a door is normal. Which words show Tom's body doing something FEAR does?

wrongAnswers.why: confused the missing word with the clue
wrongAnswers.remedy: True — 'scared' isn't written! So which words leak the fear instead?

hints: A clue is what the character's body DOES.
What does fear do to hands and voices?

reteach.say: Clues live in bodies. Fear makes hands shake and voices vanish — so when the text says 'his hands were shaking and he couldn't speak', it's showing us fear without naming it. Point at those words: that's your evidence.

block.text: I think Tom is scared ___ the text says his hands were shaking.

wrongAnswers.why: joined the parts without showing the clue is the REASON
wrongAnswers.remedy: The clue is WHY you think it. Which joining word gives a reason — remember Lesson 20?

wrongAnswers.why: picked a contrast word for a reason
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'But' shows a difference. The shaking hands don't disagree with the fear — they PROVE it. Which word means 'here's my reason'?

hints: The clue is your REASON for thinking it.
Which joining word introduces a reason?

reteach.say: The proof stem runs on 'because' — the reason word from our conjunctions lesson. What I think… BECAUSE… the clue. 'I think Tom is scared BECAUSE the text says his hands were shaking.' The 'because' glues the idea to its evidence.

block.definition: the reason word — it glues your idea to your clue
block.example: I think… because the text says…

practiceBank.skill: make an inference with the full stem

block.prompt: 'Nina peeped round the door. She tiptoed past the sleeping baby and held her breath.' What is Nina trying to do? Prove it with the stem.
block.sample: I think Nina is trying to stay quiet so the baby keeps sleeping, because the text says she tiptoed and held her breath.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: She's trying to keep quiet / not wake the baby — because the text says she tiptoed and held her breath.

wrongAnswers.answer: She is playing hide and seek
wrongAnswers.why: answered from imagination, not the text's clues
wrongAnswers.remedy: Fun idea — but which words support it? Check the clues: tiptoed, held her breath, SLEEPING baby. What do quiet feet near a sleeping baby tell us?

wrongAnswers.why: idea without evidence — the proof is missing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Now prove it! Which words show the quietness? Add 'because the text says…'.

hints: Why would someone tiptoe and hold their breath near a SLEEPING baby?
Use both parts: I think… because the text says…

reteach.say: Stack the clues like a detective: tiptoed — quiet feet. Held her breath — quiet everything! Sleeping baby — someone she mustn't wake. Stack them up and the answer appears: Nina is keeping quiet so the baby sleeps on. Now say it with the stem: I think… because the text says…

block.title: Stack the clues
steps: Clue 2: held her breath → extra quiet
Worked out: she mustn't wake the baby!

block.prompt: 'Sam pulled on his wellies and grabbed his umbrella before he stepped outside.' What's the weather like — and what's your proof?
options: Rainy — wellies and an umbrella are rain things
Rainy — the text says it is raining
block.explain: The text never names the weather — but wellies + umbrella are rain gear. Worked out from clues!

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Rainy — wellies and an umbrella are rain things

wrongAnswers.answer: Rainy — the text says it is raining
wrongAnswers.why: right idea, wrong proof — claims the answer is written when it isn't (retrieval habit)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Hunt for the word 'raining' in the sentence. Not there! Your idea is right — so what are the real clues?

wrongAnswers.why: clue doesn't match the idea — people go outside in all weathers
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check the clue against the idea: do you grab an UMBRELLA for sunshine? What is an umbrella for?

hints: What are wellies and umbrellas FOR?
The weather word isn't written — the objects are your clues.

reteach.say: Inference isn't only feelings — you can infer the weather, the place, the time! Sam's things do the talking: wellies are for puddles, umbrellas are for rain. The sentence never says 'raining', but the rain gear leaks it. Objects are clues too.

practiceBank.skill: match the clue to the feeling

block.prompt: Match each clue from a story to the feeling it leaks.

pairs.left: punched the air and did a little dance
checked her watch again and again

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: air-punch→delighted, dragged feet→miserable, shaking hands→terrified, watch-checking→worried

wrongAnswers.why: not picturing the action — matching at random
wrongAnswers.remedy: Act it out! Drag your feet with your head down… does your body feel delighted doing that? What does it feel?

hints: Act each clue out with your body — the feeling follows.
Start with the one you're surest of and cross it off.

reteach.say: Your body is a clue-decoder. Act the words out: punch the air — joy bursts out! Drag your feet — glum. Shaking hands — fear. Watch-checking — worry, worry, worry. When you're stuck on a clue, perform it, and the feeling names itself.

block.caption: Act the clue — feel the feeling

practiceBank.skill: make an inference with the full stem

block.prompt: 'Aisha punched the air and did a little dance when she saw her spelling score.' How does Aisha feel about her score? Full proof, please.
block.sample: I think Aisha feels delighted because the text says she punched the air and did a little dance.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Delighted/proud/thrilled — because the text says she punched the air and did a little dance.

wrongAnswers.why: invented a detail the text never gives — answering beyond the evidence
wrongAnswers.remedy: Careful, detective — does the text tell us the score? We only know how she FEELS about it. What do her actions leak?

wrongAnswers.why: reason from opinion, not from the text
wrongAnswers.remedy: Maybe! But your proof must come from the words on the page. Which ACTIONS show the happiness?

hints: What do her actions — air punch, little dance — leak?
Both parts: I think… because the text says…

reteach.say: Stick to what the words give you. The text shows two actions — punched the air, did a little dance — and actions like that leak one thing: she's over the moon about that score. We can't know the number; we CAN prove the feeling. I think Aisha is delighted because the text says she punched the air and danced.

rows: air punch + dance are in the text
the text never says the score

block.prompt: 'The bell rang for playtime. Jack grabbed his football and looked at the door.' What will Jack do next? Prove it with a clue.
block.sample: I think Jack will run outside to play football, because the text says he grabbed his football and looked at the door.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: He'll go out to play football — because the text says he grabbed his football and looked at the door.

wrongAnswers.why: prediction ignores every clue in the text
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check the clues: playtime bell, football in hand, eyes on the door. Where is everything pointing?

wrongAnswers.why: good prediction but the proof is missing
wrongAnswers.remedy: I think you're right — now show me WHY. Which words point that way? 'Because the text says…'

hints: Where is everything pointing — the bell, the ball, the door?
A prediction is an inference about what's NEXT. It still needs its clue.

reteach.say: Predicting is inferring forwards. Line up the clues like arrows: the bell says playtime NOW, the football says what he wants to play, the door says where he's heading. All three arrows point one way — out to the playground. And your proof is those very words.

block.title: Arrows to the answer
steps: Clue: the bell rang for PLAYTIME → it's time to play
Clue: grabbed his FOOTBALL → what he'll play
Clue: looked at the DOOR → where he's going
Inference: he'll run out to play football!

practiceBank.skill: infer two feelings, each with its own clue

block.prompt: Stretch! 'Poppy's lip wobbled as the lights went out. Then her big sister took her hand, and Poppy let out a giggle.' Find TWO feelings — each with its own clue.
block.sample: First I think Poppy feels frightened because the text says her lip wobbled when the lights went out. Then I think she feels safe and happy because the text says she giggled when her sister took her hand.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Frightened at first (lip wobbled in the dark), then safe/happy (giggled when her sister took her hand).

wrongAnswers.why: missed that the feeling CHANGES across the passage
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read the first sentence by itself — what does a wobbling lip in the dark leak? Now the second — what changed?

wrongAnswers.answer: Scared then happy, because her sister came
wrongAnswers.why: second feeling right but the clue is a retell, not the text's words
wrongAnswers.remedy: Nearly! Point to the exact words that show the happy — what did Poppy DO when her sister took her hand?

hints: Take one sentence at a time — one feeling each.
Two stems: 'First I think… because…' then 'Then I think… because…'

reteach.say: Characters' feelings can flip mid-story — so we track them clue by clue. Sentence one: lip wobbles, lights out — fear creeping in. Sentence two: sister's hand, a giggle — fear melts, safe and giggly. Two feelings, two clues, two little proofs. That's expert-level detecting.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave feeling-proofs with prediction and two-feeling items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the clue words highlighted in the passage, then a level-1 clue-spotting item.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ full-stem answers across levels 2–3 where the clue matches the idea, including one non-feeling inference (weather or prediction) → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'inference with evidence'.
struggleProtocol: Name why ('the clue is missing' / 'the clue doesn't match the idea').
Highlight the clue words together in the passage.
One hint: 'Finish the sentence: because the text says…'.
Re-ask with a loud, easy clue (Mai's huge grin), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Keep the casebook frame; let rewards match the learner's interests (badges, stars, stickers). Swap interestSlots nouns (pet, sibling, sport) where marked — never the clues or answers.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable proof with a loud clue; praise the process — 'you matched every idea to its clue from the text.'

differentiation.support: Clue pre-highlighted in the passage; the stem card stays on screen; one feeling at a time.
differentiation.stretch: Infer two feelings with two separate clues (l22-p09); infer a character's NEXT action and defend it.

extension: Home case: find a clue in a favourite storybook tonight and prove one character's feeling to a grown-up using the stem.
assessmentEvidence: Child answers an inference question with the full stem — a sensible idea plus a located, matching clue from the text.
revisitLater: The stem returns verbatim in the Lesson 25 review; use one inference proof as a starter in Lessons 23–24 (instructions lessons).
